doc.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: How to play for singers
summary: He explains following rather than leading singers, voicing away from the melody, and differences among Joe Williams, Ella and Sarah Vaughan, naming great pianist accompanists.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: And how do you play for singers?

Well the thing is you’ve got to know how to follow them, not lead them. One of the main things you do for singers — because most of the singers use the Great American Songbook — I hate to keep saying that but the Great American Songbook is the way of life, as I said before. If Art Tatum and Charlie Parker played it, who are we not to? Bird never wrote any — Bird wrote a couple of blues numbers [scats] and rhythm. Mostly everything that Charlie Parker played was “You and the Night and the Music” and “In the Still of the Night” or “April in Paris.” They played standards. I’ll tell you they played standards. Keith Jarrett’s playing standards. Case closed you see. So to play for singers, the one thing I tell piano players, the one thing you don’t do if you’re playing for a singer, and the singer’s singing [scats] if the singer is singing on the major sixth, [sings] “will I ever find” Sarah Vaughan. You don’t voice the chord. You always try to voice the chord with the leading tone not being in the top part of the voice. Because if you do that then you’re no longer accompanying. If you’re playing the leading tone that she’s singing, you orchestrate the way Nelson Riddle did with Frank Sinatra. See I think that, of myself as an orchestra because the piano is an orchestra. I play a little embellishment. That’s how you play for a singer. Now some singers, Joe Williams loved the single line, like Count Basie. A note here and then a space. Ella Fitzgerald might like you to [scats]. Big band sound. Sarah Vaughan might like a combination of both you see. So you have to know how to do it with all of them and you do this by listening to them. So if you get a call for the gig already you know when to hold and when to fold. So it’s really not that hard a thing. Then when you get an opening then you do your arpeggios or you do your big chord thing or whatever. And that’s the thing. See that was the beautiful thing about playing for Joe Williams because anything I’d do he could follow me. I could never throw him off, because he could hear. You wouldn’t throw him off. And then he’d sing behind the beat and I’d have to go straight ahead. I couldn’t wait, because if I waited for him to try to — we’re going to be wrong. Just follow the swallow, and keep doing what

you’re doing, I’ll meet you at the end you see. So that’s really what I tell young piano players. Some of the greatest piano players I know are the ones the played for singers, like Tommy Flanagan, like Hank Jones, like Oscar Peterson. Oscar Peterson with Billie Holiday, great accompaniment. Oh yeah. Like Ellis Larkins. Like my hometown, who Hank Jones says is probably number one, Jimmy Jones, who did orchestrations for Duke, who played on that famous record with Sarah Vaughan with Clifford Brown or Joe Benjamin or Paul Quinichette and Herbie Mann. That’s Jimmy Jones with those lush, beautiful chords. And see I’ve always been attracted to chords. I love chords you know. Plus I did a lot of listening to George Shearing who is one of my heroes. That’s why I said harmonically speaking you know the people talk about Bill Evans but I’ve always been more involved with George Shearing’s harmonic gestures, you know. And then there was a blind pianist who passed away named Chris Anderson from Chicago who was Charlie Parker’s favorite piano player, who taught Herbie Hancock, because nobody really talks about it. I’m just here to tell you the truth. As a matter of fact I was told that Bill Evans used to come and check out Chris Anderson, which he did, because he was totally unique. He was a harmonic genius.
